passages.title: Oaths by the morning light and the still night: your Lord has not forsaken you
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are Allah's answer to a silence. Revelation had paused, the Prophet ﷺ was hurting, his enemies were mocking — and Allah swears by the light of the morning and the stillness of the night that He has neither walked away from His Messenger nor come to dislike him. What holds the passage together is a single movement: two oaths taken from the sky (ayat 1–2), a double denial that lifts the accusation (ayah 3), and then two promises that reach far past the present moment into the Hereafter (ayat 4–5).

## The moment behind the words

This is one of those passages where knowing the occasion unlocks everything.

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded from Jundub that the Prophet ﷺ became ill and so did not stand for prayer for a night or two. A woman then came and said, "O Muhammad! I think that your devil has finally left you" — meaning, mockingly, that the being she imagined was inspiring him had abandoned him. So Allah revealed *By the forenoon. By the night when it darkens. Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you.* Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir all recorded this hadith, and identifies the narrator as Jundub ibn 'Abdullah Al-Bajali Al-'Alaqi. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, on the basis of other reports, that the woman who taunted him was Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab.

There is a second strand in the same reports. Ibn Kathir cites a narration from Al-Aswad bin Qays, who heard Jundub say that Jibril was slow in coming to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, at which the idolaters said, "Muhammad's Lord has abandoned him" — and this passage came down. Al-'Awfi likewise reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Jibril was delayed for a number of days, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **was affected by this**, and that the idolaters began saying, "His Lord has abandoned him and hates him." That small phrase — that he was affected by it — is where the human weight of the sūrah sits. The pain was not only the taunting; it was the absence itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles an apparent tension between the reports with care. The narration in Bukhari from Jundub mentions the illness that kept him from rising at night for tahajjud but says nothing about a break in revelation; the narration in Tirmidhi mentions the break in revelation but not the missed night prayer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes these are not conflicting: the same narrator may simply have related one incident on one occasion and the other on another. It further notes that a delay in revelation occurred twice — once in the very early stage of the call, known as *fatrah al-waḥy*, "a temporary break in the revelation," which was the longest period; and another time when, according to one narration, the pagans (or the Jews) asked about the soul and he ﷺ promised an answer the next day but omitted to say *insha'Allah*, after which revelation ceased for some days and the taunting began.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān prefaces all this with a scene from the same narration of Jundub recorded by Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi: a finger of the Prophet ﷺ was wounded and bled, and he said that it was only a finger bleeding, and whatever it suffered was suffered in the cause of Allah. Set beside the taunt, the contrast is telling. Physical injury he brushed off. The thought that his Lord had turned away was another order of pain altogether — and it is *that* which Allah addresses.

## Why swear by the morning and by the night?

The reply does not begin with an argument. It begins with an oath — and the two things Allah swears by are chosen with exact care.

**Aḍ-ḍuḥā** is the forenoon: the part of the morning when the sun has climbed and the light is full. Ibn Kathir says simply that in this ayah "Allah is swearing by the forenoon and the light that He has placed in it."

**Al-layl idhā sajā** — "the night when it *sajā*." Ibn Kathir explains *sajā* as meaning that the night settles, darkens, and overcomes; he attributes this to Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and others. Note that the first word in that gloss is *settles* — the night is not merely arriving but coming down fully and covering everything over.

The pairing is the point. Ibn Kathir says this is "a clear proof of the power of the Creator of this (light) and that (darkness)," and connects it to Allah's words, *By the night as it envelops. By the Day as it appears* (92:1–2), and to *(He is the) Cleaver of the daybreak. He has appointed the night for resting, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. Such is the measuring of the Almighty, the All-Knowing* (6:96). Read those two ayat with Ibn Kathir's comment and the argument is already made: the night is not a lapse in Allah's power over the day. It is appointed and measured by the same One who cleaves the daybreak. He swears by both, because both are His.

## "Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you"

Ayah 3 answers the taunt twice over, once for each half of the accusation.

*Mā waddaʿaka rabbuka* — Ibn Kathir glosses it plainly: "He has not abandoned you."

*Wa mā qalā* — Ibn Kathir glosses: "He does not hate you."

Now set that beside what was actually being said. In Al-'Awfi's report from Ibn 'Abbas, the idolaters were saying, "His Lord has abandoned him and hates him." Two charges — and the ayah strikes down both, in the same order they were made. Nothing is conceded, and nothing is left standing.

Notice, too, who is being addressed. The enemies spoke *about* him, in the third person: "Muhammad's Lord has abandoned him." Allah speaks *to* him, in the second: *your Lord.*

And notice what is *not* said. The passage does not deny that revelation paused, nor that he was ill, nor — in Ibn 'Abbas's words — that he was affected by it. What it denies is the meaning his enemies read into it. Delay is not desertion. This is the heart of the passage for anyone who has ever taken a hard stretch as a verdict on how Allah sees them.

## Ayah 4: what is coming is better than what is here

*And indeed the Hereafter is better for you than the present.* Ibn Kathir explains: "the abode of the Hereafter is better for you than this current abode." He then draws out how the Prophet ﷺ lived this: he "used to be the most abstinent of the people concerning the worldly things, and he was the greatest of them in his disregard for worldly matters" — something Ibn Kathir says is known by necessity from his biography. He mentions that when the Prophet ﷺ was given the choice at the end of his life between remaining in this life forever and then entering Paradise, or moving on to the company of Allah, he chose what is with Allah over this lowly world. (Ibn Kathir does not name a collection for this, so we relate it as he does.)

Ibn Kathir supports the point with a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was lying on a straw mat that left marks on his side; when he rose he rubbed his side, and Ibn Mas'ud asked leave to spread something soft over the mat. He replied that he had nothing to do with this world, and that the likeness of himself and this world is a rider who rests in the shade of a tree, then passes on and leaves it. Ibn Kathir notes that At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah both recorded this hadith by way of Al-Mas'udi, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih." A rider does not renovate the shade. He rests in it and moves on.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two readings of ayah 4, both worth holding:

- Taking *ākhirah* in its familiar sense of the Hereafter and *ūlā* as this present world, the ayah tells the Prophet ﷺ not to be disturbed by the pagans' taunts: they will see even in this world that their assumptions and accusations were absolutely false, and in the Hereafter he will be blessed with divine favours to his heart's content, far more than what he will receive in this fleeting world.
- Taking *ākhirah* in its primitive sense of "the later state or condition" against *ūlā* as "the former state or condition," the ayah means that every succeeding moment of the Prophet's ﷺ life is better than the one before it — including progress in knowledge and wisdom, in degrees of nearness to Allah, and in the economic and political fields as well.

## Ayah 5: a promise deliberately left open

*And verily, your Lord will give you so that you shall be well-pleased.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to what is missing: Allah does not specify here *what* He will give him. "The statement is open and general." The measure named is not a quantity but a state — he will be granted everything he desires, so much that he will be pleased. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists among the things he desired: the progress of Islam, the general spread of Islam in the world, the fulfilment of every need of the Ummah, his own triumph over his enemies, and the raising of the word of Allah in the land of the enemy.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah of the final abode: there Allah will give him until He pleases him "concerning his followers," and in what He has prepared for him of His generosity — including the River of Al-Kawthar, which will have domes of hollowed pearls on its banks, and whose mud will be the strongest fragrance of musk. He also cites a report of Ibn 'Abbas recorded by Imam Abu 'Amr Al-Awza'i, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was shown what his Ummah would be blessed with after him, treasure upon treasure, and he was pleased with that, whereupon this ayah was revealed; and that Allah will give him in Paradise one million palaces, each containing whatever he wishes. Ibn Kathir states that this was recorded by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, that the chain is authentic to Ibn 'Abbas, and that statements of this kind can only be said from *tawqīf* — meaning information the Prophet ﷺ himself conveyed.

Now feel where the ayah lands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, citing Qurtubi, that when this ayah was revealed the Prophet ﷺ said that in that case he would not be pleased so long as a single member of his Ummah remained in the Fire. He took a promise made *to him* and spent it *on us*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates, in a narration from Sayyidna 'Ali, that his intercession for his Ummah will be accepted, and that Allah will ask him, "O Muhammad, are you pleased?" and he will answer, "My Lord, I am pleased." (This narration is given without a named collection, so we relate the teaching without attributing it to one.)

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Muslim, from Sayyidna 'Amr Ibn al-'As, that the Prophet ﷺ recited the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) — *So, one who follows me is surely mine, and the one who disobeys me, then You are Most Forgiving, Very Merciful* (14:36) — and then a verse containing the words of 'Isa (peace be upon him), *If You punish them, then, they are Your slaves* (5:118); then he raised his hands, wept, and prayed, "O Allah, my ummah, my ummah!" Allah sent Jibril to ask why he was weeping, and he replied that he sought his ummah's forgiveness; and Jibril was sent back to inform him that Allah has pardoned them, and that Allah would please him and would not displease him regarding his ummah.

Read the sūrah again with that in place. It opens with a man mocked for being abandoned, and it arrives at a Lord who will not let His beloved be displeased about *us*.

## Living it

**Read your own night as night, not as verdict.** The accusation the enemies made — silence means rejection — is the same one a struggling believer makes against himself. Ayah 3 refuses it. The Prophet ﷺ himself lived through a pause in revelation, and Allah's own answer was that this meant no abandonment and no dislike from his Lord.

**Take the oath seriously as an argument.** Allah could have said only "your Lord has not forsaken you." He first pointed at the morning light and the settled night — which Ibn Kathir calls a clear proof of the power of the Creator of both. The same Hand that appoints the dark cleaves the daybreak.

**Let ayah 4 reorder your accounting.** If the later is better than the earlier, then loss now is not the final line of the ledger. Ibn Kathir's chosen image, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, is the calibration: a rider in the shade of a tree, who rests and then passes on.

**Let ayah 5 make you hopeful, not passive.** The promise is open and general by design. And the one to whom it was made made his own pleasure conditional on his Ummah — which should produce in us both love for him ﷺ and a serious desire not to be the ones he has to weep over.

passages.title: Three past favours: orphanhood sheltered, wandering guided, need satisfied
passages.tafsir:
**Sūrah 93:6–8 — "Did He not find you as an orphan then sheltered you? Did He not find you unguided then guided you? And did He not find you needy then satisfied your needs?"**

This passage is Allah's answer to a wound, delivered not as an argument but as a memory. Having just told His Messenger ﷺ that his Lord has neither forsaken him nor hates him, Allah now turns him to look back over his own life — three times, at three moments of helplessness — and to notice who was there each time. What holds these three ayat together is a single repeated shape: a lack, and then Allah filling it. Orphaned, then sheltered. Unaware, then guided. In need, then made need-free.

*Background, briefly.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole passage this way: in response to the unbelievers' taunts, it was briefly mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ has already been blessed with many Divine favours, and the sūrah then elaborates on three of them in particular. Ibn Kathir preserves what the taunt was. Imam Ahmad recorded from Jundub that the Prophet ﷺ became ill and did not stand for prayer for a night or two, and a woman came and said, "O Muhammad! I think that your devil has finally left you" — Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir all recorded this Hadith. In another narration Jundub says that Jibril was slow in coming to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so the idolaters said, "Muhammad's Lord has abandoned him." Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Jibril was delayed for a number of days, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was affected by this, and the idolaters began saying, "His Lord has abandoned him and hates him."

That is the accusation these three ayat answer. Not with theory — with a record.

## The shape of the three

Ibn Kathir titles this stretch of the sūrah simply: a mention of some of Allah's favours upon the Messenger — "Enumerating His favours upon the Messenger ﷺ, Allah says..." All three come in the form of a question rather than a statement, so that the one addressed supplies the answer himself from his own life. And all three are built on one verb, *wajada*, "to find": Allah found him in a condition, and did not leave him in it. Ayah 6 opens with the questioning form *alam yajidka* — "Did He not find you...?" — and ayat 7 and 8 continue with *wa wajadaka*, the same finding, three times over.

## Found an orphan, then sheltered (ayah 6)

Ibn Kathir lays out the bare facts. His father died while his mother was still pregnant with him. His mother, Aminah bint Wahb, died when he was only six years old. He then came under the guardianship of his grandfather, 'Abdul-Muttalib, until his grandfather died when he ﷺ was eight. Then his uncle, Abu Talib, took responsibility for him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail that sharpens the hardship: his father died before he was born, leaving no wealth or property to look after him. And yet the ayah does not say Allah found him an orphan and pitied him. It says *fa-āwā* — He sheltered you, gave you a refuge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what that shelter looked like on the ground: the Prophet ﷺ received such deep love and affection from his grandfather 'Abd-ul-Muttalib, and after him from his uncle Abu Talib, that they took care of him more than their own children. He lost the two people who owed him care, and was given two more who gave it beyond obligation.

Ibn Kathir does not stop at childhood. Abu Talib continued to protect him, assist him, elevate his status, honour him, and even restrain his people from harming him — on to the time when he ﷺ was forty years of age and Allah commissioned him with prophethood. And here Ibn Kathir pauses over something striking: even with all this, Abu Talib continued to follow the religion of his people, worshipping idols. All of this took place by the divine decree of Allah, he says, and His decree is most excellent. That is worth sitting with. Allah shelters His Prophet ﷺ through the hands of a man who never accepted his message. The protection was real, and it was Allah's, whatever the instrument.

Then Abu Talib died a short time before the Hijrah, and, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the foolish and ignorant people of the Quraysh began to attack him. One shelter closed; Allah opened another. Allah chose for him to migrate away from them to the city of Al-Aws and Al-Khazraj among those who helped him in Al-Madinah. When he arrived at their city, they gave him shelter, supported him, defended him and fought before him — may Allah be pleased with all of them. Ibn Kathir's summary of the whole arc is the point of the ayah: all of this was from Allah's protection for him, guarding over him and caring for him.

So the shelter of ayah 6 is not a single childhood rescue. It is a chain — grandfather, uncle, then a whole city — and Ibn Kathir attributes every link of it to Allah's protection and care.

## Found unaware, then guided (ayah 7)

This is the ayah that most needs care, and the sources address it directly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Arabic word *ḍāll* carries two meanings: (1) stray, and (2) unaware — and that here it stands for the second. The ayah signifies that before Muhammad ﷺ was commissioned as a Prophet, he was unaware of the Divine Sharīʿah; he was granted the station of prophethood, and thus was guided. Ibn Kathir renders the ayah "He found you unaware and guided you," and our translation gives "unguided": both point the same way. This is about knowledge not yet given, not about misguidance departed from.

Ibn Kathir grounds this by placing beside it another ayah of the Qur'an: *And thus We have sent to you a Ruh from Our command. You knew not what is the Book, nor what is Faith. But We have made it a light wherewith We guide whosoever of Our servants We will* (42:52). What he ﷺ did not have was the Book and the knowledge of faith — and Allah is the one who sent it, and made it a light by which He guides whom He wills.

Set against the taunt, the force of this is plain. The complaint was that revelation had gone quiet. Ayah 7 reminds him that revelation came in the first place because Allah gave it, unasked — the same Lord of whom the sūrah has just said, *Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you.*

## Found in need, then made need-free (ayah 8)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word for us: *ʿāʾil* is derived from *ʿāʾilah*, which means "to be in need." The ayah signifies that Allah found him impoverished and enriched him. Ibn Kathir gives the same sense with an added dimension: "you were poor having dependents, so Allah made you wealthy and independent of all others besides Him." Two things at once — relief from want, and independence from everyone but Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names how it happened. It came about in the beginning through a business partnership with Sayyidah Khadijah al-Kubra, may Allah be pleased with her; then, once she became his wife and Mother of the Faithful, her entire wealth was devoted to his service. The pattern of ayah 6 shows itself again: in these sources, Allah's provision arrives through people, and the people are themselves part of the gift.

Ibn Kathir follows his gloss with two hadith that set the measure of this wealth. In the Two Sahihs it is recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Wealth is not determined by abundance of possessions, but wealth is the richness of the soul." And in Sahih Muslim, from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever accepts Islam, is provided with his basic needs, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him, then he will be successful." Read by that measure, the enrichment of ayah 8 is enough in the hand and a heart that no longer needs more — which fits what Ibn Kathir says of him elsewhere in this sūrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most abstinent of people concerning worldly things and the greatest of them in his disregard for worldly matters.

And Ibn Kathir draws out one more thing from the sequence of poverty and wealth: Allah combined for him the two positions — the one who is poor and patient, and the one who is wealthy and thankful.

## Where the three are pointing

These favours are not recited for their own sake. Ibn Kathir shows that the three commands which follow answer them one by one, in order. *Therefore, treat not the orphan with oppression* — meaning, just as you were an orphan and Allah sheltered you, do not oppress the orphan; do not humiliate him, scorn him or despise him, but be kind and gentle to him. Qatadah's phrasing is unforgettable: "Be like a merciful father to the orphan." *And repulse not the one who asks* — meaning, just as you were astray and Allah guided you, do not scorn the one who asks for knowledge seeking to be guided. And *proclaim the grace of your Lord* — meaning, just as you were poor and needy and Allah made you wealthy, then tell about Allah's favour upon you.

So ayat 6–8 are the memory, and what follows is what the memory obliges.

## Living it

**Read your own life the way Allah turned His Prophet ﷺ to read his.** The answer this passage gives to the feeling of being abandoned is not a new proof; it is an honest look at the past. Where were you when Allah found you, and who covered you?

**Do not read a pause as a verdict.** The taunt came during a silence. What Allah put against it was the record of favour, and the plain words *Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you.*

**Let mercy received become mercy given.** By Ibn Kathir's reading, the one who was an orphan is precisely the one told not to crush the orphan, and the one who was taught is the one told not to turn away the seeker.

**Measure enrichment correctly.** If wealth is the richness of the soul, then *fa-aghnā* — "He made you need-free" — is worth asking Allah for in whatever bracket you happen to live: enough in the hand, and contentment in the heart.

passages.title: Three answering duties: the orphan, the beggar, and proclaiming the blessing
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These three ayat are the surah's answer to itself. Everything before them was Allah speaking *to* His Prophet ﷺ — swearing by the forenoon and the settling night that He has not abandoned him, promising him a better hereafter and a gift that will leave him well-pleased, and then counting out three specific mercies from his own life: *Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? And He found you unaware and guided you? And He found you poor and made you rich?* (ayat 6–8).

Now, in ayat 9–11, the direction turns. Three gifts become three duties, and they are handed back in the same order they were given.

## The hinge word: "therefore"

Ayah 9 begins with a small Arabic particle that carries the weight of the passage: *fa* — "so", "therefore". It is not a new subject; it is a conclusion drawn from the three favours just listed. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān renders the opening accordingly: *Therefore, as for the orphan, do not oppress him.*

Ibn Kathir heads this section of his commentary with exactly that question — *How should this Bounty be responded to?* — and then reads each command as the mirror image of the gift that precedes it:

- **Ayah 9 answers ayah 6.** "Just as you were an orphan and Allah sheltered you, then do not oppress the orphan."
- **Ayah 10 answers ayah 7.** "Just as you were astray and Allah guided you, then do not scorn the one who asks for knowledge seeking to be guided."
- **Ayah 11 answers ayah 8.** "Just as you were poor and needy, and Allah made you wealthy, then tell about Allah's favour upon you."

That is the architecture of the passage, and it is worth pausing on. The response to being sheltered is not simply to be grateful in the abstract — it is to become shelter for someone else in the position you once occupied. The response to having been guided is to be patient with the person still searching. The response to having been enriched is to speak. Mercy received is meant to become mercy given, in the same currency.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān treats these three ayat as three injunctions, numbering them in turn, and draws the same backward link at two points: on ayah 9 it glosses, "Since you were a poor orphan, and Allah sheltered you, do not oppress the orphan"; on ayah 11, "just as you were poor and needy, and Allah made you wealthy, then talk about Allah's favours upon you." The full three-way mirroring is set out explicitly by Ibn Kathir.

## Why this consolation ends in commands

To feel the force of it, remember what occasioned the surah. Imam Ahmad recorded from Jundub that the Prophet ﷺ became ill and did not stand for prayer for a night or two, and a woman came and said, "O Muhammad! I think that your devil has finally left you." So Allah revealed *By the forenoon. By the night when it darkens. Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you.* Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir all recorded this hadith. In another narration from Jundub, Jibril was slow in coming to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the idolaters said, "Muhammad's Lord has abandoned him." Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when the delay came the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was affected by it, and the idolaters began to say, "His Lord has abandoned him and hates him" — so Allah revealed *Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hates you.*

So this is a surah of comfort delivered in a moment of public mockery and private grief. And notice how the comfort ends: not with rest, but with work. The one who has been reassured is turned outward toward the orphan, the asker, and the telling of Allah's favour. That is a pattern worth carrying: consolation in Islam does not terminate in the self.

## Ayah 9 — "So do not oppress the orphan"

**The word.** The verb here is *taqhar*, from *qahr*. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān defines it plainly: *qahr* means "to treat people who are less powerful in an unfair and cruel way." The word already contains the power imbalance — the definition itself locates the wrong in what the stronger does to the weaker. And an orphan, by definition, has no father standing behind him.

**What it forbids.** Ibn Kathir spells it out: "do not humiliate him, scorn him or despise him. Rather, you should be kind and gentle to him." Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān adds the material dimension the word also covers: "do not seize their wealth by force and squander it. Do not scorn them, humiliate them or despise them."

Read those two lists together and you see that the prohibition runs from the financial to the personal. Seizing and squandering an orphan's wealth is *qahr*. So is scorn, humiliation, contempt. The ayah does not rank them.

**Qatadah's standard.** The commentary does not stop at prohibition. Qatadah said: *"Be like a merciful father to the orphan."* This is the positive form of the command, and it is a very high bar — not a guardian, not a benefactor, not someone who is technically not oppressive. A *father*, and specifically a merciful one. The orphan is to be given back, as far as a human being can give it, the thing he actually lost.

**From the Sunnah.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān reports that the Prophet ﷺ said the best house of a Muslim is the one in which there is an orphan who is treated kindly, and with love and affection; and the worst house is the one in which there is an orphan who is treated badly. Ma'ārif notes this is transmitted by Bukhari in *Al-Adab al-Mufrad*, and by Ibn Majah and Baghawi, as quoted by Mazhari.

Two things to notice. First, the measure of a home is not its prayer schedule or its reputation but how the most defenceless person inside it is treated. Second, the same house that could be the *best* is, by the same presence, capable of being the *worst*. Taking an orphan in is not itself the virtue. How he is treated afterwards is.

## Ayah 10 — "nor repulse the beggar"

**The word.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān explains that *tanhar* is derived from *nahr*, which means "to scold." Again the offence is located in manner, not just in outcome. The ayah is not primarily about whether you give; it is about how you speak to someone who has had to ask.

**Who is the *sā'il*?** Here the commentaries open the word up in slightly different directions, and it is worth hearing both.

Ibn Kathir, keeping the mirror with ayah 7 ("He found you unaware and guided you"), reads it first of the one who asks for knowledge: "do not scorn the one who asks for knowledge seeking to be guided." He then cites Ibn Ishaq on the same ayah: "This means do not be oppressive, arrogant, wicked, or mean to the weak among Allah's servants." And he cites Qatadah: "This means respond to the poor with mercy and gentleness."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān states the breadth of the word directly: *sā'il* means "one who asks," and "it includes a person who asks people's wealth, that is, a beggar, and it also includes the one who asks a question of knowledge, that is, an academic investigator. The Holy Prophet ﷺ has forbidden to berate either of them."

So the word covers two kinds of poverty — the empty hand and the empty mind — and the ayah protects both.

**What to do when you have nothing to give.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān gives unusually concrete guidance here. "The best course of action is to give the beggar something. If one is unable to give a beggar anything, one should at least apologise to him politely" — the reason given is so as not to give him any further grief. Empty-handedness is not an excuse for harshness. A refusal delivered gently is still an act of respect; a refusal barked out is what the ayah forbids.

**For teachers.** Ma'ārif continues: "anyone who is searching knowledge and asks questions, it is forbidden to respond to him harshly and unkindly. The teacher should reply kindly and politely." And then a balancing qualification that keeps this from becoming naïve: "However, if the investigator is unreasonable in his approach, it is permissible to scold him to the degree that is necessary."

Two things in that sentence are worth holding together: the permission is tied to the questioner being *unreasonable in his approach*, and it is capped at *the degree that is necessary*. The default the passage sets remains kindness.

## Ayah 11 — "And proclaim the blessings of your Lord"

**The word.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān explains that *haddith* comes from *taḥdīth*, which means "to talk." Not to boast, not to announce — to *talk about*. The favour of your Lord is to become a subject of your speech.

**The meaning.** Ibn Kathir: "just as you were poor and needy, and Allah made you wealthy, then tell about Allah's favour upon you." Ma'ārif states the principle behind it: "Talking about Divine favours to people is one way of thanking Allah."

This is the third answer, and it completes the pattern. The orphan is answered with shelter, the asker with gentleness, and the gift itself with speech.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites two narrations here:

Abu Dawud recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever is not thankful to the people, then he is not thankful to Allah."* At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and said "Sahih."

Abu Dawud recorded from Jabir that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever overcomes some test (i.e., calamity) and mentions it (to others), then he is indeed thankful. And whoever conceals it, then indeed he was ungrateful."* Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud was alone in recording this hadith.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān brings two further reports of its own, by separate routes. It states the principle first — "If a person has done something good to another, he should be thanked" — and then reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever is not thankful to people on their favours is not thankful to Allah," noting this as transmitted by Ahmad with reliable authorities, as quoted by Mazhari. This is an independently cited report, not the same transmission as Ibn Kathir's. Ma'ārif then reports, transmitted by Al-Baghawi from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah as quoted by Mazhari, that the Prophet ﷺ said whoever has done good to you, you ought to return the good; and if you are unable to return the pecuniary good, then praise him in public, because he who praises people in public fulfils his moral obligation.

Put together, these show that gratitude in this religion is *audible*. It moves from the heart to the tongue, and it is owed both to Allah and to the people through whom His favour arrived — for whoever is not thankful to the people is not thankful to Allah.

**A caution the surah itself sets.** Because ayah 11 is grounded in ayah 8 — *He found you poor and made you rich* — it is worth remembering how Ibn Kathir defines that wealth. He says Allah "made you wealthy and independent of all others besides Him," and that Allah thereby combined for the Prophet ﷺ two stations: the poor man who is patient, and the wealthy man who is thankful. Ibn Kathir then cites, from the Two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Wealth is not determined by abundance of possessions, but wealth is the richness of the soul."* And from Sahih Muslim, from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr: *"Whoever accepts Islam, is provided with his basic needs, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him, then he will be successful."*

So the "blessing" you are told to proclaim is not a balance sheet. It is what Allah has done for you — including contentment itself.

## The ruling on gratitude, and what it looks like

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws a ruling from this ayah, citing Mazhari: "It is obligatory to offer gratitude to Allah on every favour He has bestowed. (But the way of offering gratitude may be different.)" The examples given are precise:

- If Allah has granted a person wealth, a part of that wealth may be spent with sincerity in Allah's way.
- If Allah has given a person a strong body, that bodily strength may be used in fulfilling the divine obligations.
- If Allah has granted a person divine knowledge, he should impart it to others.

This is what keeps ayah 11 from collapsing into talk. *Ḥaddith* means speak — but Ma'ārif's ruling makes clear that the blessing is also thanked by being *used* in the direction it was given. Knowledge kept is not thanked. Strength spent on nothing is not thanked.

## Living it

Read as a whole, ayat 9–11 give a believer a very short and very demanding list:

1. **Look at who is beneath you in power, and be gentle there.** *Qahr* is defined by the imbalance — unfair, cruel treatment of those who are less powerful. Wherever you are the stronger party — over a child, an employee, a dependent, anyone without an advocate — that is exactly where this ayah applies. Qatadah's standard is a merciful father, not merely a fair one.
2. **Guard your tone with anyone who has to ask.** The beggar and the student are joined in one word. Give if you can; apologise politely if you cannot; answer the question kindly. Ibn Ishaq's phrasing is worth keeping: do not be "oppressive, arrogant, wicked, or mean to the weak among Allah's servants."
3. **Say what Allah has done for you.** Out loud, to people. And thank the human beings through whom good reached you — because whoever is not thankful to the people is not thankful to Allah.

There is one more thing the sequence teaches, quieter than the three commands. Every one of these duties is assigned to someone who was once on the receiving end. The Prophet ﷺ is told not to oppress the orphan as one who was himself an orphan and sheltered, not to scorn the seeker as one who was himself guided, to speak of blessing as one who was himself enriched. Your own history of need is not something to be left behind once Allah lifts you out of it. It is your qualification.

## A closing note on the surah

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records here that it is sunnah to recite the *takbīr* at the beginning of every surah from Sūrat aḍ-Ḍuḥā to the end of the Qur'an. The wording, according to Shaykh Ṣāliḥ al-Miṣrī, is *lā ilāha illā Allāh wa Allāhu akbar* — "There is no god except Allah and Allah is the greatest." Ma'ārif notes a difference of practice: according to Ibn Kathir the takbīr may be recited at the end of every surah, and according to Baghawi once at the beginning of every surah; either way, it adds, the requirement of the sunnah is fulfilled. And Allah knows best.

Ma'ārif also offers a closing observation about the shape of the Qur'an itself: in most surahs from Sūrat aḍ-Ḍuḥā to the end, Allah's special favours upon the Prophet ﷺ and his special virtues and characteristics are mentioned, while a few of these surahs mention the Day of Judgment and its conditions. The earlier part of the Qur'an asserts the greatness and authenticity of the Qur'an; the later part asserts the greatness of the one to whom it was revealed.

Which makes this ending fitting. A surah that began by defending the Prophet ﷺ against the taunt that his Lord had left him closes by putting three quiet duties in his hands — and, through him, in ours.
